events.title: East India Company shifts Indian indigo to Bengal
events.summary: After Gujarat's export trade had been lost to American colonial producers, the East India Company organised experiments to revive Indian indigo in Bengal. Production was at first a Company monopoly; Company servants then set up their own factories, whose output was for some years sold compulsorily to the Company and used for remittances home. Tradition names a Frenchman, Louis Bonnaud, as Bengal's first European planter (c. 1777) near Chandernagore, but that attribution rests on secondary sources.
events.significance: Indigo became what the Imperial Gazetteer called 'the pioneer planting industry of India' and a main channel for remitting colonial profits to Britain.

events.title: Advances, debt and violence: the ryoti system in Lower Bengal
events.place: Nadia, Jessore and Barasat districts, Bengal
events.summary: Planters got almost all their indigo from peasant cultivators (ryots), who took a yearly cash advance and contracted to sow part of their land. The advance rarely covered costs, so debts piled up and passed down through families. Planters also cultivated some land directly (nij). In July 1860 the magistrate Ashley Eden told the Indigo Commission the cultivation was 'always compulsory' and submitted an abstract of 49 serious cases (murder, riot, arson, dacoity, plunder, kidnapping) from 1830 to 1859.
events.significance: Coercion through advances is the direct cause of the 1859-60 revolt.

events.title: Indigo Revolt (Nil Bidroho) begins in Nadia
events.place: Nadia district, Bengal (now West Bengal, India / Bangladesh)
events.summary: In March 1859 the ryots of a village in Nadia district agreed to stop growing indigo. The strike spread to the other indigo districts of Lower Bengal, including Jessore. Planters had pushed or forced ryots to sign contracts to grow indigo instead of food crops on their best land, and paid them less than rice would have earned.
events.significance: One of colonial India's first large peasant movements, and it ended indigo planting in Lower Bengal.

events.title: Act XI of 1860 and the Indigo Commission
events.summary: A bill read for the third time on 31 March 1860 (Act XI of 1860) enforced that season's indigo contracts by summary process and set up a commission of enquiry. events.title: Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan
events.summary: Dinabandhu Mitra's Bengali play Nil Darpan ('The Indigo Planting Mirror') was written in 1858-59 and published in 1860. An anonymous English translation ('by a Native', usually attributed to Michael Madhusudan Dutt) was printed in Calcutta in 1861. Its introduction describes a peasant proprietor forced by the indigo system to take advances until he became 'a serf and a vagabond'.
events.significance: The play made the planters' abuses known in India and Britain and is still central to how the revolt is remembered in Bengal.

events.title: Rev. James Long convicted of libel for publishing Nil Darpan
events.summary: The Anglican missionary James Long had the English translation of Nil Darpan printed and circulated. Planters' interests prosecuted him for libel in July 1861. He was convicted, sentenced to one month in jail and fined Rs 1,000. The Bengali writer Kaliprasanna Singha paid the fine at once.
events.significance: The trial kept the indigo question in public view and fed early Indian press and political opinion.

events.title: Indigo moves to Bihar; tinkathia fixed at 3 kathas per bigha
events.summary: After the Bengal revolt the industry moved from Lower Bengal to Bihar and the United Provinces. In Bihar most indigo was grown under the asamiwar contract: at first peasants had to plant 6 kathas of every bigha. After peasant agitation in 1867-68 the government cut this to 3 kathas, which became the tinkathia system. From the 1860s planters also bought up peasants' private land for direct (nij or zirat) cultivation.
events.significance: Tinkathia, the 3/20 obligation, lasted until 1918, and Gandhi took it up in 1917.

events.title: Peak of Indian indigo: about 1.7 million acres, record exports
events.place: British India (Bihar, Madras, United Provinces, Punjab)
events.summary: The official agricultural returns put British India's indigo area at 1,705,977 acres in 1894-95, the highest in the series. The crop forecast for that year estimated a yield of about 237,500 cwt. Exports hit a record 187,337 cwt worth Rs 5.35 crore (about GBP 3.57 million) in 1895-96. Bihar and the rest of Bengal Presidency shipped 109,000 cwt of the 1896-97 total and Madras 44,000 cwt.
events.significance: This is the high point before synthetic indigo arrived. Within a decade exports fell by more than four-fifths.

events.significance: The collapse fell first on factory labourers and on cultivators contracted to grow the crop.

events.summary: From 1 April 1903 Japan raised the duty on Indian indigo from 12.953 to 21.422 yen per picul. events.significance: Japan was an important outlet for Indian indigo. Tokushima's own sukumo industry was declining at the same time because of imported Indian and synthetic dye.

events.title: Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha against tinkathia
events.summary: At the request of the cultivator Rajkumar Shukla, Gandhi went to Champaran in April 1917 to investigate indigo tenants' complaints. Under tinkathia a tenant had to plant 3 of every 20 parts of his land with indigo for the landlord. Charged under Section 144, Gandhi appeared in Motihari court on 18 April 1917 with about 2,000 people outside. The case was withdrawn, and volunteers took nearly 4,000 statements in a month. A government inquiry committee with Gandhi as a member reported on 4 October 1917.
events.significance: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India and, in his words, the country's 'first object lesson in Civil Disobedience'.

events.title: Barth measures Kano's indigo-cloth economy
events.summary: Barth reported that Kano's main commerce was cotton cloth woven and dyed in the city and nearby towns, including dark-blue women's turkedi and the black litham (rawani baki). He estimated exports to Timbuktu alone at 300 camel-loads a year worth 60,000,000 kurdi (cowries), and all cloth sold abroad at no less than 300,000,000 kurdi, at a time when a family could live on 50,000-60,000 kurdi (GBP 4-5) a year. The emir levied 700 kurdi on each of the 'more than two thousand' dyeing pots in the town.
events.significance: The best quantitative snapshot of a large African indigo-cloth industry before colonial rule.

events.title: Kano cloth for the Tuareg 'Blue People'

events.title: Yoruba adire: from Abeokuta tie-dye to hand-painted adire eleko
events.summary: Adire, indigo resist-dyed cloth made by Yoruba women, first appeared as a distinct type in Abeokuta. Adire eleko, with designs painted in cassava starch before dyeing, is dated to no earlier than about 1910 and grew popular in the 1920s on imported European cotton shirting. Ibadan became the centre for hand-painted cloths. Popular designs included Olokun ('goddess of the sea') and the Jubilee pattern made for George V's 1935 jubilee. Buyers came from Nigeria, the Gold Coast, Senegal and the Belgian Congo.
events.significance: Shows a women-run indigo industry built on imported cloth and credit that sold across West and Central Africa.

events.title: Adire crisis: caustic soda, synthetic indigo and the Alake's ban
events.summary: In the Depression, newcomers used synthetic indigo and caustic soda, which led to quality complaints and a collapse in demand for adire. In the 1930s Alake Ademola of Abeokuta banned caustic soda and synthetic dye, and the women dyers hired lawyers and petitioned colonial officials. Byfield dates the collapse of the industry to 1937-39.
events.significance: Shows synthetic indigo reaching an African dye industry through local and colonial politics, not only through price.

notes: SCOPE: India under Company and Raj (1770s-1947) plus living indigo traditions of East/Southeast Asia and Africa. Synthetic-era chemistry is only touched for context.

OCR: many primary quotes come from Internet Archive OCR text of scanned Government of India volumes (Agricultural Statistics, Statistical Abstracts, Reviews of the Trade of India), the Imperial Gazetteer and Barth. Quotes are the OCR text with light normalisation (whitespace, obvious letter substitutions such as 'hiyh' to 'high'). Table-row 'quotes' reproduce raw OCR, stray characters included, so readers can match them against the page images. Ambiguous digits are listed in each series' notes.

IMPERIAL GAZETTEER: links go to the DSAL page image (vol. III: p.70 = object 105, p.71 = 106, p.74 = 109, p.75 = 110, p.182 = 217, p.290 = 325). Quotes were checked against the Internet Archive OCR of the same edition: https://archive.org/details/the-imperial-gazetteer-of-india-volume-3 . The Gazetteer's p.74 export values for 1886-87 and 1896-97 are garbled in OCR ('37 crores', '4-k crores'), so only quantities are used from that passage.

DATES: where a web page shows no publication date (Britannica, Tokushima Prefecture, Shikoku University, V&A, Google Arts & Culture, Japanese Wiki Corpus, adireafricantextiles.com, WATJCentre), the source 'date' is the 2026 access year.

OCR CORRECTIONS IN QUOTES: 1914-15 area is printed '146,060' in the OCR; the same sentence gives a decrease of 23,000 from 169,000 and the 1925-26 general summary gives 146 (thousand acres), so it is read as 146,000. Barth's 'Kan6' is rendered Kano and Ashley Eden's 'blunder' as 'plunder' (OCR errors).
FISCAL YEARS: Indian series use April-March years. 'year' is the first calendar year and 'period' gives the label (e.g. 1895-96).
TWO AREA BASES: agricultural returns (series british-india-indigo-area) and crop forecasts (series outturn; Watt 1908) give different acreages for the same year. Do not mix them in one chart line.

NOT VERIFIED / LEFT OUT: (1) Bengal's share of world indigo supply in the early 19th c. (claims such as '95% of Britain's imports by 1810' were seen only in search snippets without a fetchable authoritative page). (2) Louis Bonnaud 1777 rests on Wikipedia citing a school textbook (PENDING). (3) 'Japan Blue' coined by R. W. Atkinson in 1875: no primary text; he was in Japan from 9 Sept 1874 (PENDING). (4) 'Samurai Blue' has no documented link to indigo and was left out. (5) The Kano Chronicle was checked (Palmer 1908 translation) but no mention of the 1498 dye-pit founding was found; 1498 is a site tradition. (6) Egyptian indigo under Muhammad Ali, Soninke/Mande dyers, Fouta Djallon, Sierra Leone gara, Cameroon ndop, Assam Strobilanthes cusia, Moroccan and Lao indigo: searched, but only dealer, blog or encyclopedia-summary sources turned up, so no events were created. The Met Museum lists a Bamileke ndop royal display cloth (acc. 2013.1140.15, early-mid 20th c.), but its API record does not name indigo.

LINKS BETWEEN REGIONS: Indian trade reviews show Japan as a major buyer of Indian indigo (7,200 of 12,400 cwt in 1921-22) and Japan's 1903 tariff increase on Indian indigo. Tokushima Prefecture attributes the collapse of Awa sukumo to imports of Indian precipitated indigo and European synthetic. Egypt and Persia were steady buyers of Indian natural indigo into the 1920s.
